query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

papers.title: Enhanced Oxidation Resistance of Ultrafine-Grain Microstructure AlCoCrFeNi High Entropy Alloy.
papers.approach: Stationary friction processing to refine microstructure (ultrafine grains) followed by oxidation tests at 850–1050 °C
papers.findings: Processed samples showed a decelerated oxidation kinetics (12–48% reduction in mass gain) compared to as‐cast samples. The ultrafine‐grained microstructure promoted the formation of a protective chromia layer and Al-rich inner oxides; unprocessed samples showed formation of spinel oxides and a less coherent scale.
papers.mechanism: Microstructural refinement increases grain boundary density, which enhances internal oxidation and promotes the formation of more protective oxide scales that control diffusion of oxygen and cations.

papers.title: Mechanistic understanding of speciated oxide growth in high entropy alloys.
papers.system: Equiatomic or near-equiatomic HEAs (e.g., CoCrFeNiMn-based systems)
papers.approach: Combination of in situ atom probe tomography (APT), high-resolution electron microscopy, and X-ray diffraction to map compositional segregation during oxidation
papers.findings: A layered oxide structure was observed starting with a Ni-enriched pre-oxide layer, then Cr2O3, and subsequent multi-oxide layers rich in Fe, Co, and Mn. The study highlights that each element’s oxidation is governed by a preferential interactivity parameter (PIP) that couples thermodynamics and kinetic diffusive behavior.
papers.mechanism: Oxidation is driven by element-specific reactivity (redox potential, cohesive energy, etc.) and diffusion kinetics, leading to hierarchically organized oxide scales where early-oxidizing species form one layer and later elements diffuse to form subsequent layers.

papers.title: High Temperature Oxidation Behavior of an Equimolar Cr-Mn-Fe-Co High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: Equimolar Cr-Mn-Fe-Co HEA produced by 3D laser printing
papers.approach: Isothermal oxidation tests at 700 °C and 900 °C; microstructural and phase analyses via XRD and EDS
papers.findings: The oxidation kinetics followed parabolic rate laws with increasing oxide thickness and mass gain at higher temperatures. At 900 °C, the oxide scale exhibited cracks and spallation, leading to the matrix being segmented and ultimately catastrophic failure.
papers.mechanism: Degradation is governed by the formation of a non-uniform, porous oxide scale that, upon reaching a critical thickness and experiencing thermal stresses, cracks and spalls. This loss of adhesion permits accelerated oxidation (via inward oxygen diffusion and outward ion migration) and explains catastrophic failure.

papers.title: Mechanisms of chemical-reaction-induced tensile deformation of an Fe/Ni/Cr alloy revealed by reactive atomistic simulations.
papers.system: FCC-type Fe40Ni40Cr20 alloy (used as a simplified model for HEAs)
papers.approach: Reactive atomistic (molecular dynamics) tensile simulations in vacuum versus a high-temperature/pressure water environment
papers.findings: In vacuum, the alloy deforms by generating Shockley partial dislocations leading to an FCC-to-HCP phase transition. Under water, oxidation of the alloy surface suppresses the formation of Shockley partial dislocations and the FCC-to-HCP transition, forcing a transition from FCC to BCC instead, which is associated with a more brittle deformation response.
papers.mechanism: Surface oxidation alters dislocation nucleation and mobility; the passivated (oxidized) surface inhibits the typical ductile deformation pathway (FCC-to-HCP) and forces the system into a BCC transformation, reducing ductility and potentially leading to catastrophic failure in stress-bearing applications.

papers.title: Effect of Post-Heat Treatment on Microstructure and Corrosion Property of Additively Manufactured AlCoCrFeNi2.1 Eutectic High-Entropy Alloy.
papers.system: Additively manufactured AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high-entropy alloy
papers.approach: Post-heat treatment studies with XRD analysis to monitor phase stability and lattice spacing changes
papers.findings: Heat treatment alleviates lattice distortions inherited from the rapid solidification during additive manufacturing, promoting a shift in the FCC peak position and potentially affecting corrosion and oxidation resistance.
papers.mechanism: Reducing lattice strain via post processing modulates elemental diffusion during oxidation, which could contribute to forming more adherent oxide layers. Although not focused solely on oxidation, these microstructural changes can influence degradation behavior at elevated temperatures.

established: Oxidation in HEAs is governed by diffusion of reactive elements (e.g., Cr, Al, Mn) to the surface and formation of layered oxide scales.
Microstructural features such as grain boundary density and lattice distortion affect the kinetics and nature of oxide layer formation.
Critical oxide scale formation and integrity are key to preventing catastrophic failure under high-temperature exposure.

approaches_tried.approach: Surface mechanical processing (stationary friction processing, UNSM) to refine the grain structure
approaches_tried.outcome: Reduction in oxidation kinetics and improvement in protective oxide layer formation was observed (12–48% deceleration in mass gain).

approaches_tried.approach: Reactive atomistic simulations under different environments (vacuum vs. water)
approaches_tried.outcome: Demonstrated that surface oxidation suppresses dislocation activities and shifts deformation mechanism from FCC-to-HCP to FCC-to-BCC, correlating with reduced ductility and possible failure.

approaches_tried.approach: Post heat-treatment of additively manufactured HEAs
approaches_tried.outcome: Reduction of lattice distortions, which may affect oxidation resistance and subsequent degradation behavior.

mechanisms: Diffusion-controlled oxidation leads to the development of multi-layered oxide scales based on the relative reactivity and diffusivity of constituent elements.
Microstructural refinement increases grain boundary density, altering diffusion pathways and enhancing scale protection.

Surface oxidation can suppress conventional dislocation-mediated deformation (e.g., Shockley partial dislocations), forcing alternate (often more brittle) phase transitions (e.g., FCC-to-BCC) under stress.
disagreements: Some studies report the formation of protective scales (chromia, alumina) while others note the formation of porous, spalling oxides (e.g., spinels, Mn-oxides) that compromise integrity.

There is debate over whether oxidation-induced failure is primarily due to mechanical spallation of the oxide layer (leading to internal oxidation) or due to changes in deformation mechanisms at the atomic scale.
open_questions: For the specific additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy, does degradation stem primarily from oxidation-induced changes in microstructure (e.g., oxide spallation and internal oxidation) or from the alteration of intrinsic deformation mechanisms (e.g., suppression of ductile dislocation pathways)?
How do the competing effects of an oxidizing versus reducing gas environment quantitatively alter the kinetics of oxide formation and the subsequent mechanical failure modes?
What are the critical exposure boundaries (temperature, gas composition, time) at which protective oxide scales transition into detrimental, spalling layers leading to catastrophic failure?
opportunities: A controlled study varying the oxidation gas composition (e.g., oxygen-rich versus reducing environments) at fixed temperatures can reveal whether the governing mechanism is diffusion-limited oxide growth or oxidation-induced suppression of dislocation mobility.

Employing in situ techniques (e.g., APT, in situ HTXRD) during controlled high-temperature exposures to monitor real-time evolution of the oxide scale and phase transformations in the Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy.

Combining post heat-treatment to modify lattice distortions with variable oxidation exposures to delineate the role of microstructure in governing degradation, with the expectation that reduced lattice strain may enhance oxide adherence, thereby delaying catastrophic failure.

A falsification criterion could be established by intentionally altering one controlled parameter (e.g., reducing oxygen partial pressure) and testing if the predicted transition (e.g., reduction in oxide spallation and shift in deformation mechanism) does not occur, which would falsify the proposed mechanistic hypothesis.

directions.direction: Investigate the role of oxide scale formation and spallation under oxidizing atmospheres using controlled oxygen partial pressure adjustments.
directions.assessment: Directly targets the hypothesis that non-uniform oxide scale development and subsequent spallation govern degradation and catastrophic failure. The physics of diffusion‐controlled oxidation and scale cohesion are well‐established and supported by evidence [PMC9026100::web::016, PMC8346963::web::008]. This study is experimentally feasible by varying oxygen partial pressure during high-temperature exposures.

directions.direction: Examine the effects of switching from oxidizing to reducing gas environments on degradation, focusing on the possibility of internal dealloying and element depletion.
directions.assessment: This approach contrasts the oxidation kinetics in oxidizing versus reducing gases to test if the degradation mechanism shifts from surface scale spallation to internal loss of critical elements (e.g. Ti, Cr) via reduction reactions. While less explored, preliminary simulation and related experimental results support changes in failure mode [open question]. It is a moderately challenging but informative experiment.

directions.direction: Utilize post‐heat treatment (lattice strain relief) on the as‐manufactured alloy to assess its effect on oxide scale coherence and degradation resistance.
directions.assessment: Building on prior evidence that reducing lattice distortions can enhance oxide adherence [PMC12735082::web::007], this study would test the hypothesis by comparing untreated and heat-treated samples under identical oxidation conditions. This directly addresses whether microstructural state governs degradation kinetics and catastrophic failure.

directions.direction: Apply surface mechanical processing (e.g., stationary friction processing) to refine the near‐surface microstructure prior to exposure.
directions.assessment: Prior work [PMC9026100::web::000, PMC9026100::web::016] shows that grain refinement and increased grain boundary density can promote the formation of protective oxide layers. This method directly tests if improved heterogeneous oxide nucleation mitigates scale spallation and delays failure. It is supported by well‐known diffusion and oxidation phenomena and is experimentally accessible.

directions.direction: Perform in situ atomistic simulations to capture oxidation-induced changes in deformation mechanisms (e.g., suppression of Shockley partial dislocations) in different gas environments.
directions.assessment: This approach uses reactive MD to bridge atomic-scale mechanisms—such as suppression of dislocation-mediated phase transitions due to oxidation—with macroscopic failure. While computationally intensive, this can provide direct insight into changes in failure pathways, linking atomic structure to catastrophic failure.
